job.style: a passage that starts from a common wrong idea and corrects it

response.passage: Many students believe that rusting is simply a layer of dirt or mud that accumulates on iron objects over time. However, rusting is actually a chemical change where iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form a new substance called iron oxide. Unlike a physical change where the material remains the same, this process permanently alters the chemical composition of the metal. While some people think only iron can corrode, many other metals also react with their environment, though they may form different protective layers. Furthermore, there is a common misconception that all metals are extremely hard solids that cannot be cut. In reality, elements like sodium and potassium are soft enough to be sliced easily with a knife. Another frequent error is assuming that all non-metals are poor conductors of electricity. While most non-metals are insulators, graphite, a form of carbon, is an excellent conductor. Finally, when metals react with acids, they do not simply vanish or turn into liquid; they undergo a chemical reaction to form new compounds and often release hydrogen gas. Understanding these properties helps us distinguish between physical changes and chemical reactions in the world around us.
response.summary: Rusting is a chemical change that creates a new substance, not just surface dirt. Metals and non-metals have diverse physical and chemical properties that defy simple generalizations.
